topic: Pink, rock and black salt carry little iodine: keep iodised salt, use less of it
angle: Swapping white salt for pink/rock salt drops the main iodine source; WHO-style guidance says less salt and iodised salt work together; excess iodine and high-dose supplements carry their own thyroid risk (Hashimoto's caution)
hook: Many of my clients switched from white salt to pink salt to eat healthier. Few of them knew what they gave up.
draft:
Many of my clients switched from white salt to pink salt to eat healthier. Few of them knew what they gave up.

Iodine. Your thyroid needs it to make its hormones. India chose decades ago to add iodine to common salt, and that's how most of us get enough without ever thinking about it.

Here's the catch. Pink salt, rock salt and black salt usually carry very little iodine unless it has been added. The colour and the "natural" label don't change that. When salts on shop shelves were tested, the non-iodised ones had only a small fraction of the iodine in iodised salt. And in pregnant women, those who used non-iodised salt had lower iodine levels than those who used iodised salt. That research shows a link, so it can't prove cause, but the direction is consistent.

In my practice, the switch to pink salt is something I see again and again.

Two things are true at the same time. Most Indians eat more salt than global guidance recommends. And the salt we do eat should be iodised. Eating less salt and using iodised salt work together.

More iodine isn't better either. Too much has been linked to thyroid autoimmunity, and thyroid experts warn against high-dose iodine and kelp supplements, especially if you already have a thyroid condition.

What I'd suggest:

1. Cook with iodised salt every day. If you love pink or rock salt, keep it for a sprinkle on top, alongside iodised salt.
2. Use less salt overall, whichever kind you pick.
3. Keep iodised salt in its closed packet, away from the stove. Iodine fades with time, heat and moisture.
4. Don't start iodine or kelp supplements on your own, especially with Hashimoto's. Ask your doctor first.
5. If you take thyroid medicine, keep taking it as prescribed. Salt helps prevent a gap. It doesn't replace your tablet.

Which salt is in your kitchen right now?

#ThyroidHealth #Hashimotos #WomensHealth
